Why Does God Allow Suffering?

by Faith Eng

“How can God be good when there is so much suffering in the world?”

This is a valid question. Christians believe that God is completely good and in ultimate control of our lives. How do we reconcile that idea with all the pain and suffering we see and experience?

There are answers to these questions, but not surprisingly, they can feel complex. Some experiences of suffering are on an individual, family or community level. Others are on a much larger scale.

There are many factors to consider, but the bottom line is: The Bible shows us that suffering actually points to (rather than disproves) the existence of a good God who cares about people.

The Bible shows us very clearly that God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life. To understand how this can be true, we’ll look at the overall story of God’s relationship with people in the Bible and where we are in that story now.

So if suffering is part of your reality right now, hopefully you will find fresh hope as you see God’s plan to end suffering once and for all.

Life’s Challenges

Why Worship a God Who Allows Suffering?

Share this article

Q: "Why worship a God who allows horrible things, like a child being raped?"

There probably is no greater violation than a child being raped. It’s devastating to the victim in so many ways. When coming to terms with it, rage is appropriate. There is no explanation for such actions.

However, it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it. It is not his fault that fathers molest their daughters or that mothers verbally abuse their sons.

We human beings are pretty much free to do as we choose.

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent other people from doing evil to us?

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent us from doing evil to other people?

We might wish that God established a set of boundaries, beyond which people would be punished. We might suggest that God kill any man who molests a child.

Well then, how about the producers of child porn that might have helped motivate the man to molest the child? Would it be right if maybe God killed them too?

Ok, what should God do with, say, people who are verbally abusive? Words can wound deeply. It seems pretty apparent we get to do what we choose to do. And I don't see how we can be angry at God for letting us do that.

Hasn’t God revealed to us how to best live our lives?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 Commandments, no child would ever be raped or molested?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 commandments, nothing would ever be stolen, no spouse would be betrayed, no one's son or daughter would be murdered?

Rather than control us, God gives us freedom. God does not interfere with anyone's choices. Rather he assures us that all will someday answer for what they have done and that justice will be administered. Judgment will be based on the guidelines given.

That's one of the heaviest questions a person can ask, and I don't want to wave it away with something glib. Let me look for what grounded sources say about this before responding.I hear the weight behind this question, and I want to be honest with you rather than hand you something tidy that dodges the pain of it. So let me lay out what I found, and where the real tension stays unresolved.

**No answer fully dissolves the horror.** One source, EveryStudent, addresses this almost exactly in your terms — someone asking "why worship a God who allows horrible things, like a child being raped?" Their response doesn't try to explain away the evil itself: "There is no explanation for such actions... When coming to terms with it, rage is appropriate." That's worth sitting with — even sources trying to give an answer admit some things don't get a satisfying explanation. (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)

**The main line of reasoning offered is human freedom.** That same source argues God gives people freedom to choose, and doesn't override that freedom even when people use it to hurt others — including children: "Rather than control us, God gives us freedom. God does not interfere with anyone's choices." It also raises a hard question back: if God stopped every evil act by force, where would that line be drawn, and what would that cost in terms of freedom itself? (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)

**But that doesn't cover everything.** Cru's article distinguishes between suffering caused by human choices (sin) and suffering that isn't anyone's direct fault — a child born with an illness, a natural disaster. Sightline Ministry points to the story of the man born blind, where Jesus explicitly says it wasn't "because of his sins or his parents' sins" — some suffering just is, a byproduct of living in a world with physical laws and brokenness, not a targeted punishment or lesson. (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html; Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)

**What Christianity claims God does about it, rather than just explaining it:** thelife.com makes the point that God didn't stay distant from suffering — in Jesus, "he has given us... a down payment that he does have good reasons for allowing evil." The claim is that God entered into suffering himself through Jesus, rather than simply permitting it from a safe distance: "Though he was innocent, he voluntarily took upon himself the punishment that we deserve." (thelife, https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3)

I won't pretend that settles the ache of watching a child suffer — I don't think these sources claim it does either. What they're offering isn't "here's why it's actually fine," but something more like: the evil is real and not God's design, freedom is costly, and God's response was to enter the suffering rather than stay untouched by it.

Where does this question come from for you — is it more of a philosophical wrestling, or is there something painful and specific behind it?

happened after a game of chess. “Daddy, do you know where you’ll spend eternity when you die?” I asked him. “Well, I hope I’ll go to heaven, baby,” he replied. “Can I share with you how you can be sure?”

He said yes, and I explained how eternal security centered on him having a personal relationship with God through the forgiveness of sin Jesus offers.

“Are you ready to invite Jesus into your life and begin a personal relationship with God?”

“Yes, I am,” he said. Then he prayed and received Christ. “Mel, I feel so clean, I just feel so clean,” he said. I was in awe and amazed at what God had done — in my dad’s life and in mine.

But then death came as it often does — unexpected, unwanted and unrelenting. He passed away in his sleep a year after that prayer, at the young age of 56.

His heart just stopped beating. I was 26, and when he died, it felt like my heart stopped beating too. With his death went all the things I didn’t get a chance to do with him, to say to him.

I miss the conversations that never happened. I would have loved to talk with him about music. He was a musician at heart. He played several instruments and sang. I believe my deep love for funk bands, soul and R&B comes directly from him.

Grieving my dad continues more than a decade later. The first year was the hardest. But God held me together in the moments when I wanted to fall apart. Psalm 68:3-5 reminds me of His commitment to those who’ve lost their fathers this side of heaven.

God comforts those who grieve and mourn. He knows loss and deep grief well. He leads us to resources to help us when we lose those we love, like Journeying through Grief or the book “Experiencing Grief” by H. Norman Wright.

“We are of good courage, I say, and prefer rather to be absent from the body and to be at home with the Lord.” 2 Corinthians 5:8

When I found out my friend’s brother had passed away, also a friend of mine, I was in shock. I couldn’t really believe it. He was so young. Because I couldn’t wrap my mind around it, I also questioned Why him? Why not someone else I didn’t know? Why not somebody old and ready to go? I thought those terrible things, thinking selfishly instead of selflessly. Where did he go? I wondered. Was he sitting around, unable to wake up, waiting for the resurrection?

I had to ask someone who knew, someone who could direct me to the Scriptures. It was there that I realized that no, indeed, he wasn’t just sitting around waiting for Christ to come. In fact, he was already in Heaven. That was made clear when Jesus told the thief on the cross that he would be with Him that very day in paradise. Scripture pointed to a God who immediately accepted His children upon their death. I was comforted. What I had once seen as a curse to those on earth, perhaps even to him because he had lost out on a long life, I now saw to be a mercy, to be a blessing. To be able to stand face to face with God and enjoy in eternal delights, to be able to see the angels, to be free from sin, death, and sorrow, was to be blessed. I longed to see it for myself, realizing he had gotten to see something I had always wanted to see but still had to wait for it as I dwelt on earth. We who were grieving were the only ones suffering, not him.

Friend, are you grieving right now? Take comfort in the joy of knowing that your saved loved one is reveling in the splendor of the Lord, in His very presence, not in any type of pain or sorrow, just pure joy.

Take Action

When my dad first told me that he was not afraid to die, that he was ready to go whenever God saw fit to take him, I didn’t know what to say. I was uncomfortable with the idea of Dad dying, though I was happy for him to be at peace about it. This was probably about 5 to 10 years ago. When he did pass this last January, he told my mom he was ready to go and meet Jesus. He was 90 years old, and his body was worn out. My youngest daughter joked that God knew better than to argue with Grandpa!

When I led a small family graveside gathering in July, I focused on a Scripture that Dad often quoted from 2 Corinthians 5:6-9 which he summarized simply as “absent from the body, present with the Lord.”

So here is what we can always be certain about. As long as we are at home in our bodies, we are away from the Lord. We live by believing, not by seeing. We are certain about that. We would rather be away from our bodies and at home with the Lord. So we try our best to please him. We want to please him whether we are at home in our bodies or away from them.

My brother, who has terminal cancer, has often heard my dad talk about death in this way, so when I visited my brother, who is in hospice, I found that I was quoting Dad when my brother was grieving the loss of the close relationship he and my dad had, reminding my brother of what he had often heard Dad say. This thought also gives my brother peace about his own impending death.

The most frightening thing about death is that we are not in control. We did not choose to be born, and we do not have much choice about when we will die. Death is really an “unknown” to us except when we watch those close to us pass from this life.
sources.title: The Life :: Dealing With the Fear of Death

Before her death, my mother became convinced that the Spirit of Christ was in her, that she belonged to him, and that she would live forever with him. The very thought of what awaited her filled her with great joy.

I was there when she died — praying for her, singing Bible verses to her, and holding her hand as she let out one last soft breath. The palliative care nurse who was with me turned to me and said: “I have never seen anyone go so peacefully from this life to the next.”

In the hours leading up to that moment, my mother, in a coma, would often lift her arms up to heaven, a peaceful smile on her face. Was she seeing Jesus welcoming her into his presence forever?

When Our Day Comes

One day, it will be our turn. Our friends will meet one another and say, “Have you heard about (our name)?”

My earnest prayer for you is that when someone blurts out, “No, what happened?”, the answer will be, “(Your name) went to be with Jesus forever.”

Would you like to put your trust in Jesus and begin to experience an eternal relationship with him right now? Why not tell him so? That's what prayer is: simply telling God what is on your heart and listening to his answer.

My father’s suicide catapulted me into a time of deep grief, a time when I questioned all I thought I knew about God while clinging to him daily for the strength to get through the pain. In those first shock-filled days after I heard the news that my father had hung himself in the basement of our home, my heart would scream: “NO, NO, don’t think about it! It hurts too much!”

After the funeral, when I left to return to university, I felt so alone and overwhelmed. Whenever I had time to think, I would think of Dad and cry.

Questions and doubts started to fill my mind:

If God loved me, why had he allowed this disaster?

If God was all-powerful, why hadn’t he stopped my dad?

If God was all-knowing, why didn’t he let me know how despairing my father was? Why hadn’t he shown me how to reach him?

If God was there, why hadn’t he done something?

Was God there?

I had become a Christian a few years earlier. The thought that Jesus had died for me so I could be forgiven and enter into a personal relationship with him had filled me with surprise. I could know God? He could be closer to me than a brother? Of course I wanted to know him! Of course I wanted to be forgiven! And when, at 16, I invited him to come into my life and forgive me and change me, he had done so, filling my heart with a sense of his presence.

But now, for the first time, God had really disappointed me. And I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too. You see, my father and I had spent time together just a few days before he died, and he had asked me questions about God I couldn’t answer. Then he had asked me to transfer back to the university at home so I could be near him and I had refused to do so. Now, I wondered if he would still be alive if I had done what he wanted, and I was tormented by a deep sense of guilt.

God had really disappointed me. I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too.
sources.title: The Life :: Wrestling with God after my Father's Suicide

What they do point to, again and again, is that in Christian understanding, it's not church attendance itself that determines what happens after death — it's a person's relationship with Jesus. Let me share what these sources actually say, and I'll be clear about where the gaps are.

One story (Cru, "Forgiving My Dad Set Us Both Free," https://www.cru.org/us/en/blog/life-and-relationships/holidays/forgiving-my-dad-set-us-both-free.html) describes a father who had never had a relationship with Jesus, but shortly before he died, prayed to receive Christ — and the author describes real assurance about where he went afterward. This reflects a common thread in these sources: it's the internal turning toward Jesus, not outward religious practice like church attendance, that these writers see as decisive.

Another piece (thelife, "Finally In His Presence," https://thelife.com/devotionals/finally-in-his-presence) points to Jesus' words to the thief on the cross — a man who, as far as we know, had no religious life at all — telling him "today you will be with me in paradise." The author uses this to say that it's not about a person's track record of religious practice, but about that moment of turning toward Christ, even at the very end.

A third source (thelife, "What Kind of Eternal Life Does Jesus Offer Us?", https://thelife.com/what-kind-of-eternal-life-does-jesus-offer-us) frames it as a relationship — "the Spirit of Christ was in her, and she belonged to him" — again pointing to relationship as the key thing, not church membership.

Here's what I genuinely don't know, and I won't pretend to: I don't have a grounded answer in these sources about what happens to someone whose heart and final moments we simply don't know — where there was no conversation like the one in that first story, no clear moment we witnessed. That's a real gap, and honestly, it's one of the hardest and most tender parts of grief. Many people who love God still wrestle with not knowing, and I don't want to hand you a tidy answer that isn't actually there.

What I can say is this: you loved your dad, and the not-knowing you're carrying is a sign of that love, not a failure on your part. Would it help to talk more about him, or about what's underneath this question for you — is it more about fear, or hope, or something else?

Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

by Matt Perman

The doctrine of the Trinity is foundational to the Christian faith. It is crucial for properly understanding what God is like, how He relates to us, and how we should relate to Him.

But it also raises many difficult questions. How can God be both one and three? Is the Trinity a contradiction? If Jesus is God, why do the Gospels record instances where He prayed to God?

While we cannot fully understand everything about the Trinity (or anything else), it is possible to answer questions like these and come to a solid grasp of what it means for God to be three in one.

Use the links below to jump to a specific section:

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

Is the Trinity Contradictory?

Essence and Person

Trinitarian Illustrations?

Summary

Application

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

The doctrine of the Trinity means that there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Stated differently, God is one in essence and three in person. These definitions express three crucial truths: (1) The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, (2) each Person is fully God, (3) there is only one God.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons

The Bible speaks of the Father as God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus as God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit as God (Acts 5:3-4). Are these just three different ways of looking at God, or simply ways of referring to three different roles that God plays?

The answer must be no, because the Bible also indicates that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons. For example, since the Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), He cannot be the same person as the Son. Likewise, after the Son returned to the Father (John 16:10), the Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit into the world (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). Therefore, the Holy Spirit must be distinct from the Father and the Son.

Der Begriff „Dreieinigkeit“ oder „Dreifaltigkeit“ findet sich so nicht in der Bibel, aber er fasst gut zusammen, was sie über Gott aussagt. In der Bibel wird uns Gott vorgestellt als der Vater, der Sohn und der Heilige Geist. Gleichzeitig wird immer wieder betont, dass es nur einen Gott gibt. Die Bezeichnung „Dreieinigkeit“ trifft also den Nagel auf den Kopf! Sie drückt aus, was die Bibel uns über Gott offenbart: Dass er in drei Personen präsent ist, die doch das gleiche göttliche Wesen darstellen.

Es gibt ein paar interessante Versuche, diese Dreieinigkeit zu veranschaulichen. Nehmen wir zum Beispiel Wasser (H2O): Es existiert in verschiedenen Aggregatzuständen, nämlich als Wasser, Eis oder Dampf. Die Erscheinungsformen sind sehr verschieden, aber das Wesen ist das Gleiche: H2O. Ein anderer Vergleich ist die Wärme: Sie kann in Form von Strahlung auftreten, als Wärmestrom oder auch in festen Körpern geleitet werden.

Der Sohn (Jesus) ist ganz Gott. Der Vater ist ganz Gott. Und der Heilige Geist ist völlig ganz Gott. Trotzdem gibt es nur einen Gott. Mit unserem begrenzten Horizont ist das schwer zu begreifen. Can You Explain the Trinity?

The following clearly and briefly explains the Trinity … three gods or one?

By EveryStudent.com

Listen to article | Share this article

You and I live in a three-dimensional world. All physical objects have a certain height, width, and depth. One person can look like someone else, or behave like someone else, or even sound like someone else. But a person cannot actually be the same as another person. They are distinct individuals.

God, however, lives without the limitations of a three-dimensional universe. He is spirit. And he is infinitely more complex than we are.

That is why Jesus the Son can be different from the Father. And, yet the same.

The Bible clearly speaks of: God the Son, God the Father, and God the Holy Spirit. But emphasizes that there is only ONE God.

If we were to use math, it would not be, 1+1+1=3. It would be 1x1x1=1. God is a triune God.

Thus the term: "Tri" meaning three, and "Unity" meaning one, Tri+Unity = Trinity. It is a way of acknowledging what the Bible reveals to us about God, that God is yet three "Persons" who have the same essence of deity.

Some have tried to give human illustrations for the Trinity, such as H2O being water, ice and steam (all different forms, but all are H2O). Another illustration would be the sun. From it, we receive light, heat and radiation. Three distinct aspects, but only one sun.

No illustration is going to be perfect.

But from the very beginning, we see God as a Trinity. In the book of Genesis, the first book in the Bible, God says, "Let us make man in our image … male and female he created them."1 You see here a mixture of plural and singular pronouns.

When Moses asked God for his name, God replied, "I am" - eternally existing.

Jesus used the same phrase numerous times.

"I am the light of the world…"

"I am the bread of life…"

"I am the way, the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."

Yes, it does, because of the Trinity.

The Trinity is perhaps the most mysterious, beautiful and confounding doctrine of the Christian faith. It asserts that there is one God who exists eternally in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. While many have tried to explain the mystery with analogies and metaphors — from a three-leaf clover to the states of matter to the colors of a traffic light — the truth is all human explanations fall short. But He is also relational — being three persons — and the Father, Son and Holy Spirit have loved, interacted with and rejoiced over each other for all of eternity. In Michael Reeves’ book “Delighting in the Trinity”, he delves into this theology, explaining that he believes this is where creation came from. That's a fair question — and the language itself does sound like a contradiction on the surface, so let's unpack what's actually being claimed.

**The key distinction: "essence" vs. "person"**

According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity," the doctrine states that God is **one in essence** and **three in person**. That's the crucial move: Christians aren't saying God is one *and* three in the *same* sense. As the Spanish-language Cru resource ("Entender la Trinidad") puts it, "solo habría una contradicción si decimos que Dios es tres en la misma forma que él es uno" — there would only be a contradiction if we said God is three in the *same way* he is one. Since he's one in one respect (essence) and three in another respect (person), it's not logically contradictory — more like saying something is one *team* made of three *players*. Not a perfect analogy, but it shows the categories differ.

Cru breaks it into three claims held together:
1. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are **distinct persons** — the Bible shows them relating to one another (e.g., the Father sends the Son into the world in John 3:16; the Father and Son together send the Spirit in John 14:26 and Acts 2:33), so they can't just be the same person wearing different masks.
2. **Each person is fully God** — the Father is called God (Philippians 1:2), Jesus is called God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit is called God (Acts 5:3-4).
3. Yet there is **only one God** — not three gods, because all three share the very same divine essence.

(Source: Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief," https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)

**Some analogies people use (with caveats)**

EveryStudent's article offers a math-style way of picturing it: rather than 1+1+1=3, think of it more like 1×1×1=1 — hence "Tri-unity." They also mention illustrations like water existing as ice, liquid, and steam (all still H2O), or the sun giving off light, heat, and radiation while remaining one sun. The German EveryStudent article ("Dreieinigkeit") uses similar comparisons. But both sources are careful to say **no illustration is perfect** — these are just aids for the imagination, not full explanations.

(Source: EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity? This Article Explains It Simply," https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)

**Why Christians hold onto it despite the mystery**

Cru's article "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?" describes the Trinity as "perhaps the most mysterious, beautiful and confounding doctrine of the Christian faith" and admits that "all human explanations fall short" because "humans are limited in their understanding." The reasoning isn't that Christians invented a paradox for fun — it's that they believe the Bible itself presents God this way: fully one, yet relational within himself, with Father, Son, and Spirit loving and interacting with one another eternally.

(Source: Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?," https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html)

**Bottom line:** It's not "1 = 3" in the same sense (which would be a real contradiction), but "one *what* he is (essence), three *who* he is (persons)." It remains genuinely mysterious — Christians generally don't claim to fully grasp it, just to trust what they believe has been revealed. If you want, I'm happy to dig into any one piece of this further — like the specific Bible passages, or why this doctrine matters practically.

One of the most important features of Christian faith is accepting that Jesus is God. Christians are in trouble, then, if Jesus never made such a claim of himself! Yet many have argued that this is exactly the case: Jesus never claimed to be God, they say, and his divinity is an invention of the Christian church. Is this true?

I have found that there are two main reasons why people think Jesus never claimed to be God. Let’s take a look!

Jesus never said the exact phrase, “I am God”

Some people believe Jesus never claimed to be God because, in reading the Gospels of Jesus, they simply don’t see Jesus saying “I am God” (or something along those lines). While it’s true that the Gospels never quote Jesus saying, “I am God,” the Gospels still include statements from Jesus that clearly identify him with God. Examples include “The Father and I are one” (John 10:30) and “Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). I work through many more verses In one of my early YouTube videos, “Did Jesus really Say He was God?” While it’s always possible to reinterpret or raise skepticism over the meaning of any statement, the most natural and common-sense understanding of these quotations is that Jesus is claiming to be God.

Related: Do We “Get” Jesus?

The Gospel of John is not reliable

The second reason given to deny Jesus’s claim to divinity is this: to challenge the historical reliability of the Gospel of John. It’s well understood that John has the clearest examples of Jesus claiming to be God, and it was (probably) also the latest of the four Gospels written. So, many conclude that Jesus never claimed to be God, yet legend developed over time that he did. The earliest Gospels—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—did not include this legend because not enough time had passed. But John, which came later, has the legendary stuff. Notice how this argument admits that John presents Jesus as God, but it denies that John is a good source to use.

Some skeptics like to assert that Jesus wasn’t God — and never claimed to be. We should scratch our heads in confusion at these claims, because the Bible’s New Testament writers clearly wrote otherwise.

That's a fair and honest question — and the answer, based on the sources I found, is a bit nuanced: Jesus is never quoted in the Gospels saying the literal sentence "I am God." But there are a few places where his own words, quoted directly, make a very strong claim about his identity. Here's what's actually recorded as coming from his mouth:

**1. John 8:58** — "Very truly I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!"
This is one of the most striking. "I AM" is the name God used for himself when speaking to Moses from the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). According to Jesus Film Project's *40 Interesting Facts about Jesus* (jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts), Jesus is deliberately invoking that divine name for himself here.

**2. John 10:30** — "I and the Father are one."
Per Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god), a Greek scholar's reading of "one" here points to oneness in essence/nature, not just purpose. The immediate reaction from the Jewish leaders listening was to pick up stones to kill him for blasphemy — they clearly heard it as a claim to deity (John 10:31-33, cited via Sightline Ministry, sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god).

**3. Mark 14:61-62** — At his trial, the high priest asks him directly, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answers, "I am." This is quoted by both Cru (cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html) and Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false). The high priest's reaction was to tear his robes and cry "Blasphemy!" — again, the listeners took it as a direct claim to divine identity.

**4. John 5:17-18** — "My Father is always at his work... and I, too, am working." Sightline Ministry notes that by saying "my Father" rather than "our Father," Jesus put his own activity on equal footing with God's — which is exactly how the religious leaders around him took it, since the text says they then wanted to kill him "because he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God" (John 5:18).

So: no single verse has Jesus saying "I am God" in those exact four words. But in his own quoted speech, he uses the divine name (John 8:58), claims oneness with the Father (John 10:30), and affirms he is the Son of God under direct questioning (Mark 14:61-62) — and the people who heard him firsthand consistently understood these as claims to be God, strongly enough that they wanted to execute him for it.

I'd encourage you to read John 5, 8, and 10, and Mark 14 for yourself in context — that's really the best way to weigh what he meant. Would you like me to dig into any one of these passages more closely?

Famed nineteenth-century minister Alexander Maclaren once said, “The cross is the center of the world’s history; the incarnation of Christ and the crucifixion of our Lord are the pivot round which all the events of the ages revolve.”

As the hour of Christ’s death approached, the Gospels tell us that He even asked God for an alternative. He prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39b). But the Father knew that death was required to enact His plan. So why exactly did Jesus have to die?

We’ve put together a list of five reasons why Jesus had to die. This isn’t exhaustive by any means, but it should help you understand the importance of the cross.

Jesus died to cancel our debts

“When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:13-14).

Humans come into the world under an obligation to obey God. Having failed to do so (as we all do), we are under a debt for our disobedience that we cannot pay. God demonstrated His love for us by allowing Jesus to pay that debt on our behalf.

Jesus lived a sinless life, and through His sacrifice, our account can be cleared of the debt against us. His death canceled the record of our debt. There is no longer a record against those who walked with Jesus. And the debt was paid so it no longer stood between us and God.

I completely understand the frustration — it's fair to want real, checkable sources rather than confident-sounding guesses. Here are some actual pages where you can read what Christians believe about what Jesus' death accomplished:

1. **"Why did Jesus Have to die?"** – Jesus Film Project
 https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/why-jesus-had-to-die
 Explains ideas like Jesus dying to cancel humanity's debt (Colossians 2:13-14) and to rescue humanity.

2. **"What Is Justification and How Does It Work?"** – Cru
 https://www.cru.org/us/en/blog/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/justification.html
 Explains the concept of justification — that Jesus paid the penalty for sin so people can be declared righteous before God (drawing on Romans 3:23-24 and Galatians 2:16).

3. **"Step 1: The Christian Adventure"** – Cru
 https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/10-basic-steps/1-the-christian-adventure.html
 Talks about how Jesus' death "bridged the gulf between the holiness of God and the sinfulness of man," referencing Colossians 1:13-14, 20-23, and ties it to the resurrection.

4. **"Why Was Jesus Crucified?"** – Cru
 https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/why-was-jesus-crucified.html
 Discusses how Jesus' death dealt with death itself and "destroyed the devil's works," citing John 12:30-32 and 1 John 3:8.

5. **"Why Is the Resurrection of Jesus So Important?"** – Jesus Film Project
 https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/resurrection-important
 Explains why Christians see the resurrection as essential to the meaning of Jesus' death, drawing on 1 Corinthians 15.

A quick summary of the common thread across these pages: Christians generally believe Jesus' death paid the penalty for human sin (sometimes described as a "debt"), reconciled people to God, and — together with his resurrection — broke the power of death and evil.

Feel free to click through and read them directly rather than take my word for it. And if you want, I'm happy to dig into any one of these ideas (like justification, or the resurrection's role) in more depth.

To declare that the Bible has been “altered” over the centuries could mean a number of different things.

For instance, you could talk about how later scribes added punctuation markings, lower-case lettering, etc., as their Greek language evolved over time. But that is of little concern. When most people say that the Bible has been altered, they mean that the original written text has changed in content over many years, is now corrupted, and the original meaning lost.

It is very common these days to hear someone say that the Bible has been altered. This might come from a skeptic, but it also might come from followers of other religions that have spun off the Christian tradition such as Mormonism, Jehovah’s Witnesses, or Islam. In asserting that the biblical text became corrupted, they add that their religion’s holy writings have corrected the problem. And they use their holy writings to provide new spiritual insights that support their religious view.

Understanding the term “altered”

Despite certain anti-Christian motivations to challenge the Bible, we don’t have compelling reasons to believe that the modern Bible is wildly different from what was originally written. Even though we don’t have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts.

These manuscripts have some differences, and this is to be expected because of human error. But there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy. We can see what was altered.

But what if the original text was changed before a bunch of copies were made? If this happened, then all of our copies would have come from a bad text, and we would never be able to know what was originally written!

The Quran does not say the Bible has been changed. Just the opposite. It honors the Torah and the Bible. It mentions the Torah, the "Zabur" (the Old Testament and Psalms), and the "Injil" (the New Testament) many times.

When Islam began in the 7th century, 600 years after Jesus Christ, the Bible was accepted as true.

So, you might ask, has the Bible changed since the 7th century? No. All you have to do is compare today's Bible with a Bible written long ago.

We can find complete Bibles, all the way back to 300 A.D., hundreds of years before the Quran. You can find one in the London Museum, in the Vatican, and in many other places. If you compare today's Bible with the Bibles of 300 A.D., the Bible we have today is the same as then.

Did you know that there exist today nearly 25,000 hand-written copies of portions of the New Testament? As historians have compared these manuscripts, they have concluded that the New Testament we have today is at least 99.5% accurate to the original. No change.

(The .5% differences refer to spelling, but no change in meaning.)

Also, you might be familiar with the more recent archeological findings of the Dead Sea Scrolls. These were found in the caves of Qumran, just off the northwest corner of the Dead Sea.

Researchers have compared the Bible we have today with what they found, and they remained highly similar, nearly 100% identical.

Don't let anyone tell you that the New Testament or the Bible has been changed from its original writing. That simply is not historically accurate.

The Bible has not been changed.

Your uncle's concern is a really common one, and it's worth taking seriously rather than brushing off — but the evidence actually points the other way.

**Why "too many translations = lost original" isn't quite accurate:**

According to Sightline Ministry, we don't have the *original* manuscripts of the Bible (called "autographs"), but we do have thousands of *copies* (manuscripts). These copies have some differences due to human copying error, but "there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries).

**On translations specifically:**
EveryVietStudent addresses this directly — the concern that the New Testament was translated "too many times" and got corrupted along the way. But actual translations "were made directly from the original Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic based on thousands of ancient manuscripts" — not translations-of-translations-of-translations (https://www.everyvietstudent.com/a/215KinhThanh.html).

**The manuscript evidence itself:**
- We have over 24,000 handwritten manuscript copies of portions of the New Testament (EveryVietStudent, same source above).
- When these manuscripts are compared to each other, they agree word-for-word about 99.5% of the time. Most differences are things like spelling or word order, which barely affect meaning (same source; also EveryStudent, "Jesus in Islam," https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).
- Complete Bibles exist dating back to around 300 A.D., and comparing them to modern Bibles shows they're essentially the same. The Dead Sea Scrolls (ancient Old Testament manuscripts) also confirmed the text has remained "highly similar, nearly 100% identical" over time (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).

**On the "human error" question:**
Sightline Ministry notes that yes, scribes made some copying mistakes over the centuries, but "these changes do not compromise the reliability or accuracy of the Bible we use today. In many cases the changes were obvious, and scholars can identify the original reading with a high degree of confidence" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error).

So the short answer: your uncle's instinct — that ancient texts passed down by hand over centuries could get corrupted — is a fair thing to wonder about. But when you actually look at the manuscript evidence, scholars have far more material to work with for the Bible than for almost any other ancient text, and it shows remarkable consistency. That doesn't "prove" every theological claim in the Bible, but it does mean the text we have today is a well-attested, carefully reconstructed representation of what was originally written.

Would it help to look at a specific example — like a passage your uncle thinks may have been altered — so we can dig into the actual evidence together?

Or it’s based on their experience with a single Christian. In view of that, here’s a short list of misconceptions that some have about Christians. They’re untrue. 1. Christians Disagree About Everything…Right? Definite misconception! Christians do not disagree about everything.

We agree that Jesus is the Son of God, and died on the cross and resurrected so that we could believe and be saved. We agree that God calls us to love our neighbor. We agree that humankind is inherently sinful without the grace of God, and that God loves us anyway. We agree that truth matters. We agree that the gospel of Jesus is Good News to this world. We agree that the Holy Spirit is with us, and that God has spoken truth to us through His words in Scripture. These core beliefs have carried on through the generations since Christianity first began.

That isn’t to say that things don’t get messy. We are, after all, human. There are plenty of theological disagreements to go around. But at the end of the day, most Christians recognize that the majority of disagreements needn’t divide us. We are still brothers and sisters, unified through Christ.

Our unity is accomplished through the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13, Ephesians 4:3-4). Though we have disagreements, we are a family. That’s not to say there aren’t some strange uncles and wayward cousins.

2. Christians Are Opposed to Science…Right?

Definite misconception. Most Christians highly value the contributions of Science!

There are some Christians who take a strong obscurantist approach toward science, but I have not personally met one. Most of science doesn’t address things that concern faith in Christ. The speed of light, the chemistry of ammonium, the size of our sun, or the air speed velocity of an unladen swallow have little to do with the Gospel message. Yet for some reason, it remains a popular notion that Christians are hostile to science.
sources.title: Five Misconceptions of Christians

sources.text:
The Virgin Birth: Plausible, if God Exists

The Apostles’ Creed, an early creed of the Christian faith, affirms that Jesus Christ “was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.” If this belief is true, it means that Jesus’ entrance into human history isn’t just a tad different, but completely unique.

We can’t, of course, make the same kind of historical argument for the virgin birth that we can make for the resurrection. In the case of the resurrection, numerous eyewitnesses saw Jesus die and also later saw Him come back from the dead. But no eyewitness can attest to how Mary became pregnant. If Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, that event was private.

Atheists declare it to be a “biological impossibility” for a virgin woman to give birth. In one sense they’re correct: humans, like other mammals, are normally incapable of parthenogenesis (a word that derives from Greek words meaning “virgin” and “birth”). But in another sense they’re completely wrong.

Affirming the virgin birth of Christ as “miraculous” does not mean having to believe that the laws of nature have been broken or violated. Just because a virgin birth is not naturally possible doesn’t mean we rule out the possibility of there being a God not bound by the laws of nature.

Is anything impossible for the God who designed and crafted our meticulously detailed universe?

The Virgin Birth: The Ultimate Miracle?

People in the ancient world knew that human conception naturally required sexual intercourse. For that reason, they viewed Jesus’ conception by Mary to be a miracle. Joseph, the man who took Mary as his wife, certainly believed that Mary was telling him the truth when she said she had yet to be with a man.

Writes the great Christian thinker C. S. Lewis,
sources.title: Was Jesus Really Birthed by a Virgin?

Why Does God Allow Suffering?

by Faith Eng

“How can God be good when there is so much suffering in the world?”

This is a valid question. Christians believe that God is completely good and in ultimate control of our lives. How do we reconcile that idea with all the pain and suffering we see and experience?

There are answers to these questions, but not surprisingly, they can feel complex. Some experiences of suffering are on an individual, family or community level. Others are on a much larger scale.

There are many factors to consider, but the bottom line is: The Bible shows us that suffering actually points to (rather than disproves) the existence of a good God who cares about people.

The Bible shows us very clearly that God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life. To understand how this can be true, we’ll look at the overall story of God’s relationship with people in the Bible and where we are in that story now.

So if suffering is part of your reality right now, hopefully you will find fresh hope as you see God’s plan to end suffering once and for all.

Why Worship a God Who Allows Suffering?

Share this article

Q: "Why worship a God who allows horrible things, like a child being raped?"

There probably is no greater violation than a child being raped. It’s devastating to the victim in so many ways. When coming to terms with it, rage is appropriate. There is no explanation for such actions.

However, it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it. It is not his fault that fathers molest their daughters or that mothers verbally abuse their sons.

We human beings are pretty much free to do as we choose.

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent other people from doing evil to us?

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent us from doing evil to other people?

We might wish that God established a set of boundaries, beyond which people would be punished. We might suggest that God kill any man who molests a child.

Well then, how about the producers of child porn that might have helped motivate the man to molest the child? Would it be right if maybe God killed them too?

Ok, what should God do with, say, people who are verbally abusive? Words can wound deeply. It seems pretty apparent we get to do what we choose to do. And I don't see how we can be angry at God for letting us do that.

Hasn’t God revealed to us how to best live our lives?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 Commandments, no child would ever be raped or molested?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 commandments, nothing would ever be stolen, no spouse would be betrayed, no one's son or daughter would be murdered?

Rather than control us, God gives us freedom. God does not interfere with anyone's choices. Rather he assures us that all will someday answer for what they have done and that justice will be administered. Judgment will be based on the guidelines given.

I hear the weight behind this question. It's not abstract for you — it's about real children, real pain, and it deserves more than a tidy formula. Let me share honestly what these sources say, without pretending it resolves everything.

**God isn't the cause — human choice and a broken world are.** EveryStudent puts it directly: it's not God's fault that people take what's good and corrupt it — that fathers abuse, that evil happens. We have real freedom to choose, which means others' freedom can wound us terribly, and ours can wound others. ([EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html))

**Some suffering isn't even about anyone's sin — it's just the nature of a world with real physical laws.** Sightline Ministry points to the story of the man born blind: Jesus was asked whose sin caused it, and he said "It was not because of his sins or his parents' sins." Some suffering — like an accident on an icy road — happens simply because we live in a world governed by physical laws that don't pause for the innocent. God doesn't suspend gravity for good people. ([Sightline Ministry](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this))

**But here's what I think matters most in your question — you said you've never heard an answer that wasn't a dodge, and a dodge would be pure explanation.** A hurting child doesn't need a philosophy lecture; they need someone to be *with* them. thelife.com makes this point sharply: God didn't stay distant and let us suffer alone. In Jesus, God entered into suffering himself — genuinely, unbearably. "He did not just stay in heaven and say, 'OK you suckers, suffer!'... He showed us that we could trust him by appearing in human form... HE SUFFERED!" ([thelife.com](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3))

That's not an explanation that erases the "why" — it's a claim that God didn't exempt himself from the cost. Cru's material adds that suffering, oddly, doesn't disprove a good God's existence but points to God's own plan to end suffering permanently, not just explain it away. ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html))

I won't pretend that settles the ache. If a child suffers, "God will fix it eventually" can sound cold in the moment. What's actually sitting with you right now — is this about something specific you've witnessed or carried?

When my dad first told me that he was not afraid to die, that he was ready to go whenever God saw fit to take him, I didn’t know what to say. I was uncomfortable with the idea of Dad dying, though I was happy for him to be at peace about it. This was probably about 5 to 10 years ago. When he did pass this last January, he told my mom he was ready to go and meet Jesus. He was 90 years old, and his body was worn out. My youngest daughter joked that God knew better than to argue with Grandpa!

When I led a small family graveside gathering in July, I focused on a Scripture that Dad often quoted from 2 Corinthians 5:6-9 which he summarized simply as “absent from the body, present with the Lord.”

So here is what we can always be certain about. As long as we are at home in our bodies, we are away from the Lord. We live by believing, not by seeing. We are certain about that. We would rather be away from our bodies and at home with the Lord. So we try our best to please him. We want to please him whether we are at home in our bodies or away from them.

My brother, who has terminal cancer, has often heard my dad talk about death in this way, so when I visited my brother, who is in hospice, I found that I was quoting Dad when my brother was grieving the loss of the close relationship he and my dad had, reminding my brother of what he had often heard Dad say. This thought also gives my brother peace about his own impending death.

The most frightening thing about death is that we are not in control. We did not choose to be born, and we do not have much choice about when we will die. Death is really an “unknown” to us except when we watch those close to us pass from this life.

My father’s suicide catapulted me into a time of deep grief, a time when I questioned all I thought I knew about God while clinging to him daily for the strength to get through the pain. In those first shock-filled days after I heard the news that my father had hung himself in the basement of our home, my heart would scream: “NO, NO, don’t think about it! It hurts too much!”

After the funeral, when I left to return to university, I felt so alone and overwhelmed. Whenever I had time to think, I would think of Dad and cry.

Questions and doubts started to fill my mind:

If God loved me, why had he allowed this disaster?

If God was all-powerful, why hadn’t he stopped my dad?

If God was all-knowing, why didn’t he let me know how despairing my father was? Why hadn’t he shown me how to reach him?

If God was there, why hadn’t he done something?

Was God there?

I had become a Christian a few years earlier. The thought that Jesus had died for me so I could be forgiven and enter into a personal relationship with him had filled me with surprise. I could know God? He could be closer to me than a brother? Of course I wanted to know him! Of course I wanted to be forgiven! And when, at 16, I invited him to come into my life and forgive me and change me, he had done so, filling my heart with a sense of his presence.

But now, for the first time, God had really disappointed me. And I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too. You see, my father and I had spent time together just a few days before he died, and he had asked me questions about God I couldn’t answer. Then he had asked me to transfer back to the university at home so I could be near him and I had refused to do so. Now, I wondered if he would still be alive if I had done what he wanted, and I was tormented by a deep sense of guilt.

God had really disappointed me. I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too.

Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

by Matt Perman

The doctrine of the Trinity is foundational to the Christian faith. It is crucial for properly understanding what God is like, how He relates to us, and how we should relate to Him.

But it also raises many difficult questions. How can God be both one and three? Is the Trinity a contradiction? If Jesus is God, why do the Gospels record instances where He prayed to God?

While we cannot fully understand everything about the Trinity (or anything else), it is possible to answer questions like these and come to a solid grasp of what it means for God to be three in one.

Use the links below to jump to a specific section:

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

Is the Trinity Contradictory?

Essence and Person

Trinitarian Illustrations?

Summary

Application

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

The doctrine of the Trinity means that there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Stated differently, God is one in essence and three in person. These definitions express three crucial truths: (1) The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, (2) each Person is fully God, (3) there is only one God.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons

The Bible speaks of the Father as God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus as God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit as God (Acts 5:3-4). Are these just three different ways of looking at God, or simply ways of referring to three different roles that God plays?

The answer must be no, because the Bible also indicates that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons. For example, since the Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), He cannot be the same person as the Son. Likewise, after the Son returned to the Father (John 16:10), the Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit into the world (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). Therefore, the Holy Spirit must be distinct from the Father and the Son.
sources.title: Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

Dreieinigkeit - was ist das?

Frage: „Was kann ich mir unter der Dreieinigkeit vorstellen? Was bedeutet sie?“

Der Begriff „Dreieinigkeit“ oder „Dreifaltigkeit“ findet sich so nicht in der Bibel, aber er fasst gut zusammen, was sie über Gott aussagt. In der Bibel wird uns Gott vorgestellt als der Vater, der Sohn und der Heilige Geist. Gleichzeitig wird immer wieder betont, dass es nur einen Gott gibt. Die Bezeichnung „Dreieinigkeit“ trifft also den Nagel auf den Kopf! Sie drückt aus, was die Bibel uns über Gott offenbart: Dass er in drei Personen präsent ist, die doch das gleiche göttliche Wesen darstellen.

Es gibt ein paar interessante Versuche, diese Dreieinigkeit zu veranschaulichen. Nehmen wir zum Beispiel Wasser (H2O): Es existiert in verschiedenen Aggregatzuständen, nämlich als Wasser, Eis oder Dampf. Die Erscheinungsformen sind sehr verschieden, aber das Wesen ist das Gleiche: H2O. Ein anderer Vergleich ist die Wärme: Sie kann in Form von Strahlung auftreten, als Wärmestrom oder auch in festen Körpern geleitet werden.

Der Sohn (Jesus) ist ganz Gott. Der Vater ist ganz Gott. Und der Heilige Geist ist völlig ganz Gott. Trotzdem gibt es nur einen Gott. Mit unserem begrenzten Horizont ist das schwer zu begreifen. Aber schon ganz am Anfang wird Gott so beschrieben! Achtet mal auf die Pronomen im Plural schon im Schöpfungsbericht: „Und Gott sprach: Lasst uns Menschen machen nach unserem Bilde …“1

Es gibt nur einen Gott:

„Wer an mich glaubt, glaubt an den, der mich gesandt hat.“7

Can You Explain the Trinity?

The following clearly and briefly explains the Trinity … three gods or one?

By EveryStudent.com

Listen to article | Share this article

You and I live in a three-dimensional world. All physical objects have a certain height, width, and depth. One person can look like someone else, or behave like someone else, or even sound like someone else. But a person cannot actually be the same as another person. They are distinct individuals.

God, however, lives without the limitations of a three-dimensional universe. He is spirit. And he is infinitely more complex than we are.

That is why Jesus the Son can be different from the Father. And, yet the same.

That's one of the most common questions people have about Christianity, and it's a fair one to ask — let me find some grounded material on it.It's a really good question to raise, because on the surface "three" and "one" sound like they can't both be true. Here's how Christians resolve that, based on the sources I found:

**The key distinction: "one" and "three" apply to different things**

According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief" (https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html), the doctrine means "there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit." Stated more precisely: "God is one in essence and three in person." That article lays out three claims held together:
1. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons (not just three names or roles for the same individual).
2. Each Person is fully God.
3. There is still only one God.

The reason this isn't a logical contradiction is that "one" and "three" are being said in *different senses* — one in essence (what God *is*), three in person (*who* God is). A contradiction would only occur if someone claimed God was three in the very same sense he is one. As a related Cru piece on the Trinity puts it (in Spanish, "Entender la Trinidad," https://www.cru.org/mx/es/crecer-y-equipar/crecimiento-espiritual/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html): God is one *essence* — essence meaning the same as "being" — so since God is only one essence, he is only one being, not three. The three persons share that one essence rather than each having a separate one.

**Why they say the Persons are distinct, not just "modes"**

The Cru "Understanding the Trinity" article notes the Bible calls the Father God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit God (Acts 5:3-4) — but also treats them as distinct from one another: the Father sends the Son (John 3:16), the Son returns to the Father and then the Father and Son send the Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). Since one can send another, they can't simply be the same person wearing different masks.

**Some analogies people use (with the caveat that all fall short)**

EveryStudent's article "What is the Holy Trinity?" (https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html) suggests thinking of it not as 1+1+1=3, but more like 1×1×1=1 — hence the word "Trinity" (tri + unity). It also mentions common illustrations like water existing as ice, liquid, and steam, or the sun's light, heat, and radiation — three expressions, one source — while acknowledging "no illustration is going to be perfect."

Cru's article "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?" (https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html) adds an important honesty: "all human explanations fall short. Humans are limited in their understanding." It frames the Trinity less as a math puzzle to solve and more as a description of a God who is inherently relational — Father, Son, and Spirit "have loved, interacted with and rejoiced over each other for all of eternity."

So the short version: it's not a contradiction because "one" refers to God's essence/being, and "three" refers to persons within that one being — different categories, not the same claim twice. It remains genuinely mysterious, and Christians generally admit that outright rather than pretending it's fully explainable.

Does that distinction between "essence" and "person" make sense, or would it help to dig into one part more — like why Christians believe Jesus himself is called God?

Yet many have argued that this is exactly the case: Jesus never claimed to be God, they say, and his divinity is an invention of the Christian church. Is this true?

I have found that there are two main reasons why people think Jesus never claimed to be God. Let’s take a look!

Jesus never said the exact phrase, “I am God”

Some people believe Jesus never claimed to be God because, in reading the Gospels of Jesus, they simply don’t see Jesus saying “I am God” (or something along those lines). While it’s true that the Gospels never quote Jesus saying, “I am God,” the Gospels still include statements from Jesus that clearly identify him with God. Examples include “The Father and I are one” (John 10:30) and “Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). I work through many more verses In one of my early YouTube videos, “Did Jesus really Say He was God?” While it’s always possible to reinterpret or raise skepticism over the meaning of any statement, the most natural and common-sense understanding of these quotations is that Jesus is claiming to be God.

Related: Do We “Get” Jesus?

The Gospel of John is not reliable

The second reason given to deny Jesus’s claim to divinity is this: to challenge the historical reliability of the Gospel of John. It’s well understood that John has the clearest examples of Jesus claiming to be God, and it was (probably) also the latest of the four Gospels written. So, many conclude that Jesus never claimed to be God, yet legend developed over time that he did. The earliest Gospels—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—did not include this legend because not enough time had passed. But John, which came later, has the legendary stuff. Notice how this argument admits that John presents Jesus as God, but it denies that John is a good source to use.

Everything about Jesus seems confounding! At least until we begin to really look at Him, getting clear on the facts of what He did, what He taught, and what He said about Himself. More Than a Carpenter blog #whoisjesus

Jesus, Are You God?

Did Jesus say He is God? Many argue that Jesus didn’t give a definitive answer. But maybe He did! Let’s look at Jesus’ own words, as they are recorded in the Bible.

In John 5:16-18, there’s a confrontation between Jesus and a group of Jewish leaders. It’s triggered when Jesus cures a lame man on the Sabbath, the day on which Jews are forbidden to work. The Jewish leaders begin harassing Jesus. He replies, “My father is always working, and so am I.” Jesus could have said, “Our father,” but He didn’t. Jesus then adds fuel to the fire by declaring, “The Father and I are one” (John 10:30). A.T. Robertson, an esteemed Greek scholar, explains that the Greek word “one” in this passage doesn’t indicate one in person or purpose, but rather one in essence or nature. Welcome! In this post we’ll dive into whether Jesus claimed to be God.

Did Jesus claim to be just a great spiritual guide — or God in human form?

Jesus Humbly Claimed His Deity

Some skeptics like to assert that Jesus wasn’t God — and never claimed to be. We should scratch our heads in confusion at these claims, because the Bible’s New Testament writers clearly wrote otherwise.

John records that Jesus said, without ego, “Most assuredly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I AM.” At this claim of deity, the Jewish crowd grabbed stones to kill Him. Why? Because they knew that, according to Mosaic law, any person daring to make such a claim was deserving of death. They understood Jesus to be claiming that He was God.

When the high priest later asked Jesus, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” Jesus replied, “I am. And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” “Blasphemy!” cried the high priest, as he tore his robes to signal his condemnation of Jesus. “What further need do we have of witnesses?”

Jesus claimed to be worthy of the honor due God. For one simple reason. He was.

Surely only a fool would make such a claim … and yet, Jesus walked on water … calmed the wind and waves … healed the lepers … and sent demons scurrying. Could anyone but God do so?

Jesus also said that He pre-existed with God before coming to earth in human form. John 17:5 reads, “And now, O Father, glorify Me together with Yourself, with the glory that I had with You before the world existed.” In John 14:6 Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” In John 5, Jesus tells us that God the Father “has given all judgment to the Son.”

That's a really important question — and a fair one to ask. You're right that the Gospels never quote Jesus saying the literal sentence "I am God." But several passages record him saying things about himself that, in their context, function as exactly that kind of claim. Here are his own recorded words:

**1. "Before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58)**
According to Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god and sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false), Jesus here uses "I am" — the very name God gave himself to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). The reaction was immediate: the crowd picked up stones to kill him for blasphemy, showing they understood exactly what he meant.

**2. "The Father and I are one." (John 10:30)**
Cited by Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god) — the surrounding crowd's response makes the meaning clear: "You, a mere man, claim to be God" (John 10:33, as quoted by Cru at cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html).

**3. At his trial: "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answered, "I am." (Mark 14:61-62)**
Quoted by both Cru (cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html) and Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false). The high priest immediately tore his robes and cried "Blasphemy!" — again, the hearers took it as a direct claim to deity.

**4. "My Father is always working, and so am I." (John 5:16-18)**
Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god) points out that by saying "my Father" rather than "our Father," Jesus placed his own activity on equal footing with God's — and John notes the Jewish leaders wanted to kill him partly because "he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God" (John 5:18).

**5. After the resurrection, Thomas responds to Jesus by saying, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:27-28)**
Jesus does not correct or rebuke him — quoted in Jesus Film Project's article (jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts).

So to directly answer you: no single verse has Jesus saying the plain sentence "I am God." But in John 8:58, John 10:30, and Mark 14:61-62, his own recorded words carry that claim clearly enough that the people who heard him say so understood him to mean exactly that — and responded as though he'd said it outright.

Does it help to look at any one of these passages more closely, or talk about why he might have spoken this way rather than just saying it plainly?

Famed nineteenth-century minister Alexander Maclaren once said, “The cross is the center of the world’s history; the incarnation of Christ and the crucifixion of our Lord are the pivot round which all the events of the ages revolve.”

It’s obvious that Christ’s death is essential to the gospel. After all, the symbol of Christianity is the cross. But why was it so important?

As the hour of Christ’s death approached, the Gospels tell us that He even asked God for an alternative. He prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39b). But the Father knew that death was required to enact His plan. So why exactly did Jesus have to die?

We’ve put together a list of five reasons why Jesus had to die. This isn’t exhaustive by any means, but it should help you understand the importance of the cross.

Jesus died to cancel our debts

“When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:13-14).

Humans come into the world under an obligation to obey God. Having failed to do so (as we all do), we are under a debt for our disobedience that we cannot pay. God demonstrated His love for us by allowing Jesus to pay that debt on our behalf.

Jesus lived a sinless life, and through His sacrifice, our account can be cleared of the debt against us. His death canceled the record of our debt. There is no longer a record against those who walked with Jesus. And the debt was paid so it no longer stood between us and God.

Jesus died to rescue humanity

To declare that the Bible has been “altered” over the centuries could mean a number of different things.

For instance, you could talk about how later scribes added punctuation markings, lower-case lettering, etc., as their Greek language evolved over time. But that is of little concern. When most people say that the Bible has been altered, they mean that the original written text has changed in content over many years, is now corrupted, and the original meaning lost.

It is very common these days to hear someone say that the Bible has been altered. This might come from a skeptic, but it also might come from followers of other religions that have spun off the Christian tradition such as Mormonism, Jehovah’s Witnesses, or Islam. In asserting that the biblical text became corrupted, they add that their religion’s holy writings have corrected the problem. And they use their holy writings to provide new spiritual insights that support their religious view.

Understanding the term “altered”

Despite certain anti-Christian motivations to challenge the Bible, we don’t have compelling reasons to believe that the modern Bible is wildly different from what was originally written. Even though we don’t have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts.

These manuscripts have some differences, and this is to be expected because of human error. But there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy. We can see what was altered.

But what if the original text was changed before a bunch of copies were made? If this happened, then all of our copies would have come from a bad text, and we would never be able to know what was originally written!

The Quran does not say the Bible has been changed. Just the opposite. It honors the Torah and the Bible. It mentions the Torah, the "Zabur" (the Old Testament and Psalms), and the "Injil" (the New Testament) many times.

When Islam began in the 7th century, 600 years after Jesus Christ, the Bible was accepted as true.

So, you might ask, has the Bible changed since the 7th century? No. All you have to do is compare today's Bible with a Bible written long ago.

We can find complete Bibles, all the way back to 300 A.D., hundreds of years before the Quran. You can find one in the London Museum, in the Vatican, and in many other places. If you compare today's Bible with the Bibles of 300 A.D., the Bible we have today is the same as then.

Did you know that there exist today nearly 25,000 hand-written copies of portions of the New Testament? As historians have compared these manuscripts, they have concluded that the New Testament we have today is at least 99.5% accurate to the original. No change.

(The .5% differences refer to spelling, but no change in meaning.)

Also, you might be familiar with the more recent archeological findings of the Dead Sea Scrolls. These were found in the caves of Qumran, just off the northwest corner of the Dead Sea.

Researchers have compared the Bible we have today with what they found, and they remained highly similar, nearly 100% identical.

Don't let anyone tell you that the New Testament or the Bible has been changed from its original writing. That simply is not historically accurate.

The Bible has not been changed.

Ok, but what about having four Gospels? Aren't those different Scriptures, different from each other?

This is such a common and fair question — and it's worth digging into rather than just taking anyone's word for it (mine included!).

Here's what the sources say:

**The short answer: your uncle raises a real concern, but the evidence actually points the other way.**

It's true we don't have the *original* documents (the actual papyrus or parchment the biblical authors first wrote on) — those wore out or were lost long ago, as **Sightline Ministry** explains: "we don't have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries).

But that's actually true of *all* ancient literature — we don't have Plato's or Aristotle's original manuscripts either. What makes the Bible's case unusually strong is the sheer *quantity* and *closeness in time* of the copies. As **EveryStudent** notes, "there exist today nearly 25,000 hand-written copies of portions of the New Testament," and when historians compare them, "the New Testament we have today is at least 99.5% accurate to the original... The .5% differences refer to spelling, but no change in meaning" (https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html). That same source points out you can compare today's Bible to complete Bibles dating back to 300 A.D. — housed in places like the Vatican and the London Museum — "and the Bible we have today is the same as then."

**Sightline Ministry** adds an important nuance: yes, scribes made copying errors over the centuries — that's just human nature. But "there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error). Because we have so many manuscripts, scholars can spot the mistakes by comparing them against each other — it's like having thousands of witnesses to cross-check rather than relying on just one or two.

The **cadaestudiante.com (EveryStudent Spanish)** source frames the key test well: when judging any ancient document's reliability, we ask "how many copies do we have?" and "how much time passed between the original and the earliest copy we have?" (https://www.cadaestudiante.com/articulos/biblia.html). By those standards, the Bible is actually far better attested than almost any other ancient text we trust historically.

So the "telephone game" image — where a message gets more garbled with each retelling — isn't quite the right picture. It's more like having thousands of independent copies you can lay side by side and compare, which lets scholars trace back with real confidence to what was originally written.

Would you like to dig into how translations specifically work (going from the original Greek/Hebrew into English, for example)? That's a related but slightly different question your uncle might also be pointing at.

Or it’s based on their experience with a single Christian. In view of that, here’s a short list of misconceptions that some have about Christians. They’re untrue. 1. Christians Disagree About Everything…Right? Definite misconception! Christians do not disagree about everything.

We agree that Jesus is the Son of God, and died on the cross and resurrected so that we could believe and be saved. We agree that God calls us to love our neighbor. We agree that humankind is inherently sinful without the grace of God, and that God loves us anyway. We agree that truth matters. We agree that the gospel of Jesus is Good News to this world. We agree that the Holy Spirit is with us, and that God has spoken truth to us through His words in Scripture. These core beliefs have carried on through the generations since Christianity first began.

That isn’t to say that things don’t get messy. We are, after all, human. There are plenty of theological disagreements to go around. But at the end of the day, most Christians recognize that the majority of disagreements needn’t divide us. We are still brothers and sisters, unified through Christ.

Our unity is accomplished through the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13, Ephesians 4:3-4). Though we have disagreements, we are a family. That’s not to say there aren’t some strange uncles and wayward cousins.

2. Christians Are Opposed to Science…Right?

Definite misconception. Most Christians highly value the contributions of Science!

There are some Christians who take a strong obscurantist approach toward science, but I have not personally met one. Most of science doesn’t address things that concern faith in Christ. The speed of light, the chemistry of ammonium, the size of our sun, or the air speed velocity of an unladen swallow have little to do with the Gospel message. Yet for some reason, it remains a popular notion that Christians are hostile to science.
sources.title: Five Misconceptions of Christians

The Virgin Birth: Plausible, if God Exists

The Apostles’ Creed, an early creed of the Christian faith, affirms that Jesus Christ “was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.” If this belief is true, it means that Jesus’ entrance into human history isn’t just a tad different, but completely unique.

We can’t, of course, make the same kind of historical argument for the virgin birth that we can make for the resurrection. In the case of the resurrection, numerous eyewitnesses saw Jesus die and also later saw Him come back from the dead. But no eyewitness can attest to how Mary became pregnant. If Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, that event was private.

Atheists declare it to be a “biological impossibility” for a virgin woman to give birth. In one sense they’re correct: humans, like other mammals, are normally incapable of parthenogenesis (a word that derives from Greek words meaning “virgin” and “birth”). But in another sense they’re completely wrong.

Affirming the virgin birth of Christ as “miraculous” does not mean having to believe that the laws of nature have been broken or violated. Just because a virgin birth is not naturally possible doesn’t mean we rule out the possibility of there being a God not bound by the laws of nature.

Is anything impossible for the God who designed and crafted our meticulously detailed universe?

The Virgin Birth: The Ultimate Miracle?

People in the ancient world knew that human conception naturally required sexual intercourse. For that reason, they viewed Jesus’ conception by Mary to be a miracle. Joseph, the man who took Mary as his wife, certainly believed that Mary was telling him the truth when she said she had yet to be with a man.

Writes the great Christian thinker C. S. Lewis,
sources.title: Was Jesus Really Birthed by a Virgin?

That's a great question to be curious about, especially as you're getting to know her family's tradition!

Honestly, I don't have grounded source material in front of me that specifically defines the term "Theotokos" or explains how different Christian traditions view it — so I don't want to guess at that from memory. I'd rather be upfront about that gap than give you something ungrounded.

What I *can* share, from sources I have access to, is some closely related ground: the belief that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary is affirmed in the Apostles' Creed, one of the earliest and most widely shared statements of Christian faith. As Sightline Ministry notes, "The Apostles' Creed... affirms that Jesus Christ 'was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.' If this belief is true, it means that Jesus' entrance into human history isn't just a tad different, but completely unique." (Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-virgin-birth)

That belief about Mary and the virgin birth is shared broadly across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Christians — it's part of what unites them, even though, as Sightline Ministry also points out elsewhere, Christians "have plenty of theological disagreements" on other matters while still holding core beliefs about Jesus in common (Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/five-misconceptions-of-christians).

But the specific title "Theotokos," what it literally means, and how much emphasis different traditions place on Mary's role — that's a more specific point of Orthodox theology and devotion that I don't have solid grounding to speak to accurately right now. I'd rather not risk misrepresenting something that clearly matters to your girlfriend's family.
